The maximum fork length attained by Bigeye snapper, Lutjanus lutjanus, has been recorded at 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters], a size consistent with other medium-bodied members of the Lutjanidae family, which typically range from 30 to 40 centimeters in fork length across the tropical Indo-West Pacific. Field surveys across this region indicate that individuals rarely exceed this value, suggesting an asymptotic growth pattern typical of tropical reef fishes. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this length is estimated at 582 grams [Wwi = 582 grams], derived from length-weight regressions calibrated for this species in Indonesian waters. In contrast, females first achieve reproductive competence at a significantly smaller size, with the fork length at puberty measured at 12.2 centimeters [Lp = 12.2 centimeters]. The body mass of a female at this pubertal length is approximately 26 grams [Wwp = approximately 26 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic growth required between the onset of maturity and the achievement of maximum size. This pronounced disparity between size at first maturity and ultimate size underscores a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive onset, a pattern frequently observed in short-lived tropical lutjanids subject to high and variable juvenile mortality.

Reproductive output in Lutjanus lutjanus has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C]. Gravid females produce 102841 eggs per year [Ri = 102841 eggs per year], a figure representing the maximum reproductive rate recorded for this species at this thermal regime. This annual fecundity is relatively modest compared to some larger lutjanid congeners, which can produce several hundred thousand eggs per season. The corresponding maximum daily reproductive rate, when the annual total is divided across the spawning season, amounts to approximately 281.8 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 281.8 eggs per day], a value that reflects a protracted spawning period rather than a single massive event. Such a pattern of serial spawning, with females releasing batches of pelagic eggs over several months, is widespread among tropical snappers and is thought to buffer against stochastic variation in larval survival conditions across the reproductive window.

Developmental timing in Bigeye snapper is strongly influenced by ambient temperature. At a water temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilization to eclosion of the yolk-sac larva, lasts approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days]. This brief embryonation period is typical of tropical marine teleosts with small, pelagic eggs and high incubation temperatures. The hatchling emerges as a lecithotrophic larva, relying entirely on its yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth, based on a mean egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters reported for the congener Lutjanus stellatus, is estimated at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a tiny initial mass that places the species among the small-egged lutjanids. These small-bodied hatchlings are planktonic and highly vulnerable to predation during the early larval stages, necessitating rapid growth to reduce the duration of this high-risk pelagic phase.

The maximum lifespan of Lutjanus lutjanus, as inferred from mark-recapture studies and otolith ageing of specimens collected in the South China Sea, has been estimated at 4015 days [am = 4015 days] when maintained at a temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately 11 years, is moderate for a lutjanid of this body size; congeneric species such as Lutjanus campechanus can exceed 50 years in temperate waters. The relatively compressed lifespan of Bigeye snapper is consistent with a faster-paced life history, characterized by early maturity at a small fraction of ultimate size and a high annual reproductive investment. The trade-off between early reproduction and extended somatic maintenance is evident in the steep growth trajectory from the hatchling mass of 0.00032 grams to the asymptotic mass of 582 grams, a several-million-fold increase occurring over a few years.

Comparing the body mass at female puberty of 26 grams [Wwp = 26 grams] to the ultimate wet weight of 582 grams [Wwi = 582 grams] reveals that females are only about 4.5 percent of their asymptotic mass when they become reproductively mature. This extreme precocity, in which maturation occurs long before somatic growth is complete, is a defining feature of the species' life-history strategy. The fork length at which females attain puberty, 12.2 centimeters [Lp = 12.2 centimeters], also contrasts sharply with the ultimate fork length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters]. This hierarchical investment — diverting resources to gonadal development early — is a classic response to high adult mortality rates, ensuring that at least some reproductive output occurs before the increasing hazard of predation truncates the lifespan. Under a thermal regime of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of 102841 eggs per year [Ri = 102841 eggs per year] and the realised lifespan of 4015 days [am = 4015 days] combine to produce a lifetime fecundity that can sustain local populations despite intense early-life mortality.
